title: How often must hazardous materials handlers in Japan take the safety course?
description: Japan's Fire Service Act Article 13-23 safety course for licensed hazardous materials handlers: who must attend, the one and three year deadlines, evidence.
shortAnswer: Under Article 13-23 of Japan's Fire Service Act, every licensed hazardous materials engineer who handles hazardous materials at a permitted facility must attend the prefectural safety course (hoan kōshū). Article 58-14 of the Regulation on Hazardous Materials sets the timing: within one year of starting the work, then within three years from the first April 1 after each course. Handlers who hold a license but are not doing such work are not required to attend.
keyTakeaways: The duty in Article 13-23 applies to license holders actually engaged in handling hazardous materials at manufacturing sites, storage facilities and handling facilities.
The first course is due within one year of starting the work, or within three years from the next April 1 if the license was issued or a course was taken in the two years before starting.
After that, the course is due within three years from the first April 1 after the previous course, on a rolling cycle.
Unlicensed workers may handle hazardous materials at these facilities only in the presence of a Class A or Class B license holder (Article 13(3)).

Facilities must appoint a hazardous materials safety supervisor with at least six months of practical experience at such facilities; failing to do so carries up to six months' imprisonment or a 500,000 yen fine.
jurisdiction: Japan (national; courses run by prefectural governors and designated bodies)
regulator: Fire and Disaster Management Agency (FDMA) of the Ministry of Internal Affairs and Communications, prefectural governors, and municipal fire authorities
appliesTo: Licensed hazardous materials engineers (kikenbutsu toriatsukaisha) of Class A, B or C who handle hazardous materials at permitted facilities
Hazardous materials safety supervisors at facilities that must appoint one
Operators of manufacturing sites, storage facilities and handling facilities such as fuel stations, tank farms, chemical plants and factories using fuels or solvents
Supervisors who schedule licensed and unlicensed workers on hazardous materials tasks

sections.heading: Which law requires the hazardous materials safety course?

blocks.text: **Article 13-23** of the Fire Service Act (Act No. 186 of 1948) states that a licensed hazardous materials engineer engaged in handling hazardous materials at a manufacturing site, storage facility or handling facility must attend a course on the safety of handling work run by the prefectural governor, including municipal mayors and other bodies the Minister designates. As at November 2026 this is the current text on [e-Gov](https://laws.e-gov.go.jp/law/323AC1000000186).

The timing is set in **Article 58-14** of the [Regulation on the Control of Hazardous Materials](https://laws.e-gov.go.jp/law/334M50000002055) (Prime Minister's Office Ordinance No. 55 of 1959). Article 58-14(3) leaves course subjects, hours and other details to the FDMA Commissioner. The facilities themselves are defined through Article 10 of the Act, which bars storing or handling hazardous materials at or above the designated quantity anywhere other than a permitted facility.

sections.heading: Who must attend the safety course?

blocks.text: Only license holders who are actually engaged in handling hazardous materials at a permitted facility must attend. The duty attaches to the work, not to the license, so a person who holds a license but works in an office role with no handling duties is outside Article 13-23 until they start handling work.
Article 13-2 of the Act creates three license classes, issued by the prefectural governor to people who pass the national examination:

blocks.text: Article 13-3(4) limits the Class A examination to people with a qualifying chemistry degree or equivalent, or Class B holders with at least two years of practical experience in handling hazardous materials. Article 13(3) of the Act prohibits anyone without a license from handling hazardous materials at a permitted facility unless a Class A or Class B holder is present. That rule is why many facilities keep several licensed staff on each shift, and each of those staff falls under the safety course duty.

sections.heading: When is the safety course due?

blocks.text: Article 58-14 sets one rule for the first course and another for every course after it. Both use the first April 1 after a reference date as the start of a three year window.

items: **First course, general rule:** within one year of the date the person began handling work at a facility.

**First course, recent license or course:** if the license was issued, or a course was taken, within two years before the person began handling work, the course is due within three years from the first April 1 after the license date or course date.
**Every later course:** within three years from the first April 1 after the previous course, and the same rule repeats after each course.

blocks.text: Because the window starts on the April 1 after the reference date, the effective interval is a little over three years and always ends on March 31. Tracking systems should store the reference date and compute the deadline from the next April 1, rather than adding three years to the course date.

Prefectures and their designated bodies run the course, and formats vary. The [Tokyo Fire Department safety course page](https://www.tfd.metro.tokyo.lg.jp/sk/hoan_kousyu.html) describes the course as intended for license holders engaged in handling hazardous materials at manufacturing sites, storage facilities and handling facilities, held under Article 13-23. It offers an online course through electronic application, in person sessions, and separate sessions for the Tokyo islands, with part of the administration entrusted to a public interest foundation.

Online attendees in Tokyo cannot change their viewing period once set, while in person attendees can switch to another date with spare seats by phoning the fire station where they applied before 9:30 on the course day. The course sits alongside other statutory fire service courses listed on the [Tokyo Fire Department training index](https://www.tfd.metro.tokyo.lg.jp/sk/index.html), such as the fire prevention manager course.

sections.heading: What is a hazardous materials safety supervisor, and how does the role relate to the course?

blocks.text: Article 13(1) of the Act requires the owner, manager or occupant of a facility designated by Cabinet Order to appoint a hazardous materials safety supervisor (kikenbutsu hoan kantokusha) from among Class A or Class B holders with at least six months of practical experience in handling hazardous materials. Article 48-2 of the Regulation limits that experience to work at permitted facilities.

Article 31-2 of the Cabinet Order on the Control of Hazardous Materials lists the facilities that need a supervisor by excluding smaller ones. Examples of exclusions include indoor storage and underground tank storage holding no more than 30 times the designated quantity of Class 4 materials with a flash point of 40 degrees Celsius or more, and mobile tank storage.

Under Article 48 of the Regulation, the supervisor must instruct workers, including licensed handlers who stand in, so that handling meets the technical standards and the facility's safety rules, and must direct emergency measures and contact the fire service in a fire. Article 13(2) of the Act requires the appointment and any dismissal to be notified without delay. Because the supervisor is a licensed handler engaged in handling work, the supervisor is also subject to the Article 13-23 course cycle.

sections.heading: What are the consequences of missing the course?

blocks.text: Article 13-2(5) of the Act allows the prefectural governor that issued a license to order its return if the holder breaches the Act or orders under it. Failing to attend the course required by Article 13-23 is a breach of the Act, so it can expose the holder to a return order. Article 13-2(4) allows the governor to refuse a new license for one year after a return order.

For the facility, Article 42(1)(vi) makes operating without appointing a required safety supervisor punishable by imprisonment of up to six months or a fine of up to 500,000 yen. Under Article 13-24, municipal authorities can also order a supervisor to be dismissed if the supervisor breaches the Act or the arrangement threatens public safety.

sections.heading: How should an operator manage the safety course cycle?

items: Keep a register of every license holder with license class, issue date, start date of handling work and last course date.
Compute each person's deadline using the Article 58-14 rule, starting from the April 1 after the reference date.
Book courses early, since prefectural sessions can fill and in person dates are limited.
Check that each shift has a Class A or Class B holder present wherever unlicensed staff handle materials.
Record the safety supervisor's appointment, experience and course status together.
Add internal training on the facility's own procedures, since the statutory course covers general safety and legal changes, not your site.

blocks.text: [How to set mandatory training refresh cycles](/guides/how-to-set-mandatory-training-refresh-cycles) covers deadline logic, and [how to prepare training records for an audit](/guides/how-to-prepare-training-records-for-an-audit) covers the evidence pack. Operators that also ship hazardous goods in the United States can compare [DOT hazmat employee training](/regulations/dot-hazmat-employee-training), and building level duties are set out in [Japan's fire prevention manager rules](/regulations/japan-fire-prevention-manager-training).

sections.heading: How does Knowledge Foundry approach this?

blocks.text: Knowledge Foundry models Article 13-23 as an obligation that attaches when a license holder is assigned to handling work, and encodes the Article 58-14 April 1 rule so that deadlines are derived rather than typed in. Course certificates and supervisor appointments become dated evidence linked to each facility.

faqs.q: Does a license holder who changes employer restart the cycle?
faqs.a: The rule follows the person, not the employer. Article 58-14 counts from the date the person began handling work, or from their license or last course date. A new employer should check the date of the last course and compute the next deadline from the April 1 after it, rather than assuming a fresh one year period.

faqs.q: Is the safety course the same as license renewal?
faqs.a: No. The safety course is a training duty for license holders engaged in handling work. Separately, Article 34 of the Cabinet Order requires a holder to apply without delay to have the license rewritten when its particulars change. Attending the course does not update the license, and updating the license does not satisfy the course.

faqs.q: Do Class C license holders need the safety course?
faqs.a: Yes, if they are engaged in handling hazardous materials at a permitted facility. Article 13-23 applies to every licensed hazardous materials engineer doing such work, without distinguishing between classes. Class C holders cannot supervise unlicensed workers, but they are still covered by the course duty.

faqs.q: Can the safety course be taken online?
faqs.a: Some prefectures offer it online. The Tokyo Fire Department offers an online course alongside in person sessions. Arrangements differ by prefecture, so operators should check the course provider for the prefecture where the handler works.
